title: How To Capture And Hold Your Students’ Attention On Zoom ntion-on-zoom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin's core recommendation for improving Zoom lessons is disarmingly simple: stand up while teaching. He argues that standing triggers a cascade of positive changes — greater charisma, brighter energy, more natural body language — that in turn improve student attentiveness, participation, and enjoyment. He offers practical support for the shift, including using a stand-up desk, teaching from an easel instead of relying heavily on a document camera, physically moving during the lesson, and standing back from the camera so students can see gestures and body language. He also suggests inviting students to stand and mirror movements as a way to get them physically engaged. He closes by contrasting this advice with what he calls needlessly complex professional development he recently sat through, insisting that authentic, animated, in-person-style teaching — not more video content — is what students are missing most.
points: Stand up while teaching directed Zoom lessons whenever possible instead of sitting the whole period.
Use an easel or classroom whiteboard rather than relying heavily on a document camera or Zoom whiteboard.
Physically move and vary your distance from the camera so students can see body language and gestures.
Invite students to stand and mirror your movements to get them physically engaged in the lesson.
Treat the Zoom lesson like a classroom performance — plan props, movement, and energy the way you would in person.
quotes: You’re going to stand up during directed lessons. This one thing will cause you to teach more authentically and make your lessons worth watching.
It’s why top performing YouTubers rarely share their screen. They know that it’s them and their uniqueness that draws viewers and keeps them watching.
By moving a few feet away from your camera, students can see your body language and hand gestures.
Invite your students to stand and mimic your moves. Use hand gestures, body movements, and echoing to get students physically involved in their learning.

It’s hard enough for students to be separated from friends and social interaction. That they have to sit and stare at yet another screen and watch videos rather than receive real teaching is a tragedy.
